title: Optical control of the cardiac rhythm with photoswitchable Na_V1.5 channel blockers

paper_content.abstract: Voltage-gated sodium channel Na 1.5 is essential for cardiac excitability, mediating the rapid depolarization phase of the cardiac action potential (AP) and ensuring proper electrical conduction in the heart. Dysfunction of Na 1.5 is implicated in life-threatening arrhythmias, making it a critical therapeutic target. Acting as a Na 1.5 open-state blocker, quinidine demonstrates efficacy in arrhythmia treatment, but its low specificity restricts its clinical application. Here, we report an optopharmacological strategy which enables a precise and optical control of Na 1.5 function by means of photoswitchable quinidine derivatives. Through systematic structural optimization, we identify azo-Q2a as a high-performance photoswitchable inhibitor, exhibiting low activity in the dark or under 480 nm light irradiation (trans isomer), while approximately 7-fold higher efficacy is observed under 365 nm light irradiation (cis isomer). Of note, azo-Q2a demonstrates exceptional selectivity for Na 1.5 over cardiac ion channels and other Na 1 subtypes, minimizing potential off-target effects. Furthermore, by solving the cryo-EM structure of the Na 1.5 in complex with the cis-active isomer azo-Q2a (3.0 Å resolution), we reveal the essential binding site that is responsible for the optical control of Na 1.5. Finally, azo-Q2a also attenuates heart rate of living zebrafish larvae with light, showing its potential in cardiac related research and treatment. Our work not only establishes azo-Q2a as a robust photoswitchable inhibitor for Na 1.5 but also provides a structural blueprint for the rational design of next-generation optopharmacological antiarrhythmic agents.
paper_content.introduction:
The Na 1.5 encoded by the SCN5A gene is the predominant subtype of voltage-gated sodium channels family (Na 1.1-1.9) in the heart, which plays an essential role in the excitability of cardiomyocytes1. The channels mediate the sodium influx into cells resulting in inward sodium current (I ), which induces fast depolarization of rapid response cardiac action potential (AP). Therefore, dysfunction of Na 1.5 channels underlies multiple cardiac channelopathies2-4, including long QT syndrome type 3 (LQT3), Brugada syndrome (BrS), sick sinus syndrome (SSS), dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), atrial fibrillation (AF), and progressive cardiac conduction disease (PCCD). This underscores its status as a pivotal therapeutic target for rhythm management.

Additionally, given its pivotal role in action potential generation and conduction, Na 1.5 has long been recognized as a canonical pharmacological target for Class I antiarrhythmic drugs (Ⅰ ). Among them, quinidine belongs to the Ⅰ subclass as the first antiarrhythmic drug in the world. Acting as a Na 1.5 channel open-state blocker, quinidine inhibits peak I , thereby reducing the membrane excitability of cardiomyocytes, slowing down the depolarization and conduction velocity of rapid response cardiac AP. It has been previously used for conditions such as atrial premature beats (APB), paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT), AF and LQT35.

However, its therapeutic utility is severely constrained by extensive off-target polypharmacology. Quinidine often accompanies inhibition of hERGN channel, thereby prolonging APD, ERP and QT interval6,7, which increases its off-target activities8. Furthermore, quinidine exhibits promiscuous binding to multiple extracardiac receptors, including nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs)9, 5-hydroxytryptamine receptors 3 (5-HT )10 and α adrenergic receptors11. Its nonspecific pharmacodynamic profiles induce intolerable gastrointestinal (nausea, diarrhea) and neurological (tinnitus, cinchonism) adverse effects12 in approximately 20-30 percents5 of patients during clinical application. These limitations underscore the imperative for developing targeted Na 1.5 modulators with improved specificity.

Light has emerged as a powerful biophysical modality for spatiotemporally precise control of biological systems13-15. Through its integration with pharmacology, optopharmacology enables non-invasive and rapidly reversible modulation of target-specific receptors and ion channels. This innovative strategy effectively circumvents the problems of off-target and dose-limiting adverse effects of traditional drugs, and thus achieve a much more precise treatment. Moreover, optopharmacology has been widely applied in ion channels16-18, transporters19, G protein-coupled receptors20,21, receptor-linked enzymes22. Pioneering studies have demonstrated the photopharmacological modulation of cardiac sodium channels23, yet there remains a strong demand for novel compounds that exhibit optimal Na 1.5 photoswitching, guided by a deeper mechanistic understanding.

In this work, we describe a photoactivated quinidine derivative with photoswitchable azobenzene moiety incorporating, which enables reversible optical control over Na 1.5 function and heart rate. We further characterize the binding sites of our lead compound cis-azo-Q2a using single-particle electron cryo-microscopy (cryo-EM). This provides a structural template for achieving selectivity and facilitate rational photoswitchable drug design.
paper_content.results:
Rational design and synthesis of photoswitchable quinidine derivatives.
As disclosed in the recently cryo-structure of Na 1.5 in complex with quinidine24, quinidine blocks the Na 1.5 channel mainly with the quinoline moiety. While the quinuclidine group directly interrupts the central permeation pathway, the quinolone aromatic ring primarily interacts with the F1760 residue through a - stacking interaction. Much inspired by the above-mentioned crucial interaction, we hypothesized that quinidine derivatives with additional aryl substituents attached to the quinolone core would be beneficial for the binding affinity of Na 1.5.

Initially, we designed three simple quinidine phenyl derivatives with phenyl substituents at the C-2 (Q1), C-3 (Q2), and C-6 (Q3) positions of the quinoline core (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. 1a). Specifically, Q1 was synthesized from quinidine via a Minisci reaction25 while Q2 and Q3 were prepared through Suzuki-Miyaura coupling reactions with phenylboronic acid using 3-I-QD and 6-OTf-QD as starting materials, respectively26,27.

Remarkably, whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in HEK293T cells heterologously expressing Na 1.5 channels revealed that Q1 and Q3 exhibited significantly higher inhibition rates than quinidine at 10 µM concentration (8.8 ± 2.9% for quinidine, 69.5 ± 6.2% for Q1, and 44.7 ± 7.8% for Q3, Fig. 1b and Supplementary Fig. 1b). These results strongly suggest that enhanced π-π stacking interactions may strengthen the binding between quinidine derivatives and the Na 1.5 ion channel.

Next, we explored photoreactive quinidine derivatives, focusing on azobenzene-based chromophores due to their widespread application. In total, nine azo-quinidine derivatives (hereafter referred to as azo-QD) were designed, featuring azobenzene moieties installed at ortho-, meta-, and para-positions with phenyl spacers at the C-2, C-3, and C-6 positions of the quinoline core (Fig. 2a).

Notably, our synthetic approach for azo-QDs utilized Suzuki-Miyaura coupling with three key intermediates: 3-I-QD, 6-OTf-QD, and 2-Br-QD (Fig. 2). The synthesis of 2-Br-QD began with the oxidation of quinidine using m-CPBA, followed by reduction with NaHSO , yielding N-oxide QD in 45% over two steps28. Subsequent bromination via the Yu protocol afforded 2-Br-QD in 46% yield29.

For 3-I-QD, direct derivatization was achieved through Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling with azo-BPin1 and azo-BPin2, producing the desired products in 27% and 24% yields, respectively. Meanwhile, 6-OTf-QD and 2-Br-QD were successfully coupled to furnish target compounds in 86%, 48%, 38%, and 33% yields. However, attempts to employ sterically hindered azo-BPin3 in the Suzuki-Miyaura reaction failed to yield any quinidine derivatives.

Photochemical characterization of azo-QDs.
With all 6 azo-QDs in hand, photochemical characterization has been explored (Fig. 3a-b and Supplementary Fig. 1c-g). Using UV-Vis spectroscopy, we characterized the spectral properties of all cis- and trans- azo-QDs. In the dark, they existed as the thermodynamically favored trans isomer. Isomerization to the cis isomer was triggered upon UV-A irradiation (365 nm), and this process was reversed within 5 seconds upon exposure to blue light (480 nm).

Taken azo-Q2a as an example, we observed a rapid and reversable photoswitch upon oscillating between 365 and 480 nm illumination over cycles (Fig. 3c). Using 1H-NMR and 13C-NMR spectroscopy, we assessed the relative concentrations of the two isomers in equilibrium after 365 and 480 nm illumination (Fig. 3d, Supplementary Fig. 2-3). After illumination at 365 nm, trans isomer azo-Q2a was efficiently isomerized to cis isomer (86%); 480 nm illumination resulted in efficient isomerization back to the trans isomer (79%). While we noted that the isosbestic point shifts slightly upon illumination at 480 nm which is small relative to the main spectral features, this might result from minor side- or photoproduct formation or from changes in solvent polarity and ionic strength.

Furthermore, the photoisomerization rates of azo-Q2a were measured. Under 365 nm UV light at 8500 lux, the half-life was 28 min, whereas under 480 nm blue light at 1500 lux, the half-life was 3.5 min. The quantum yields of azo-Q2a were determined to be 0.075 under 365 nm irradiation and 0.32 under 480 nm irradiation. These results demonstrate that azo-Q2a exhibits efficient and controllable photoreactive behavior across different irradiation wavelengths30 (Supplementary Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 1).

Finally, we examined the chemical stability of azo-Q2a. Under in vitro conditions, azo-Q2a remained remarkably stable, exhibiting a half-life (t ) of 107 h in the absence of reducing agents (Fig. 3e). In contrast, exposure to 1 mM glutathione (GSH) triggered rapid cis-to-trans isomerization with a half-life of 59 min, driven by the reversible reduction of the -N=N- bond. At a higher GSH concentration (10 mM), azo-Q2a underwent predominant reductive degradation with a half-life of 143 min, indicating a shift in the reaction pathway under strongly reducing conditions (Supplementary Fig. 5).

Optical control of Na 1.5 channels with photoswitchable azo-QDs.
To determine whether azo-QDs support optical control of Na 1.5 channels, we initially profiled the concentration-dependent inhibition activities of quinidine and six derivatives to Na 1.5 current in the dark or under 365 nm illumination, using whole-cell patch-clamping recordings in HEK293T cells heterologously expressing Na 1.5 channels. (Fig. 4a-d and Supplementary Fig. 6a-e).

When holding the cellular membrane potential at -120 mV, the expected Na+ currents were observed at the typical voltage steps31 (-120 to -20 mV). All of the examined azo-QDs in the cis isomer conferred stronger inhibition activity than quinidine, and azo-Q1a, azo-Q2a, and azo-Q3b displayed a significant increase in their IC values after 365 nm illumination. (Fig. 4a-c and Supplementary Fig. 6a-e). Among the examined azo-QDs, azo-Q2a showed the most prominent alteration (IC = 11.76 µM in cis; 81.58 µM in trans, Fig. 4c), while quinidine had no obvious difference (IC = 35.87 µM under 365 nm; 41.21 µM in dark, Fig. 4d). IC values are detailed in Supplementary Table 2.

We measured current-voltage (I-V) steps between -120 and +40 mV (5 mV steps) in the presence of 10 µM azo-Q2a (Fig. 4e). In its cis isomer, azo-Q2a strongly suppressed inward currents conducted by Na 1.5 channels, whereas the trans isomer had no discernible effect. In addition, neither isomer altered the activation property of Na 1.5, assessed as conductance-voltage (g-V) relationships and the V value (Fig. 4f, Supplementary Table 3). Note that blockade of Na 1.5 channels was readily reversible as we repeatedly photoswitched azo-Q2a between its trans and cis isomer (Fig. 4g-h).

azo-Q2a is highly selective and significantly reduces hERG toxicity of quinidine.
To further evaluate the selectivity profile of azo-Q2a among other sodium channel subtypes (Na 1.2–Na 1.6) highly expressed in the central nervous system and muscle tissues (Supplementary Fig. 7a). At a concentration of 10 μM, cis-azo-Q2a exhibited potent inhibition of Na 1.5 (61.1 ± 4.8%, use-dependent, Supplementary Fig. 6f) but minimal activity (< 10%) against all other subtypes tested. In contrast, trans-azo-Q2a under dark conditions showed negligible suppression of Na 1.5 (2.5 ± 1.6%) yet significantly inhibited Na 1.3 (36.2 ± 6.1%). Notably, this off-target effect on Na 1.3 was effectively reversed upon optical illumination, which switches the compound to cis-configuration.

These results underscore the light-dependent selectivity of azo-Q2a for Na 1.5. Given that Na 1.5 serves as the predominant sodium channel in cardiac tissue, spatially confined illumination enables the high-affinity cis-azo-Q2a to selectively modulate heart function while minimizing potential off-target effects in neural or other systems.

In addition, recalling that quinidine’s off-target interactions that inhibit hERG channels lead to serious cardiotoxicity7, we investigated the potential inhibition activity of azo-Q2a towards other ion channels known to contribute to cardiac action potential, including K 4.3 (I ), K 2.1 (I ), hERG (I ) and Ca 1.2 (I ) channels (Fig. 5a). The experiments monitored the currents of these channels under both 365 and 480 nm illumination. Currents of these ion channels were recorded using whole-cell patch-clamping in HEK293T and CHO cell lines expressing cardiac ion channels (see Methods section for details).

The inhibition rate of 10 µM azo-Q2a for Na 1.5 channels was significantly different between the cis (61.1 ± 4.8%) and trans (2.5 ± 1.6%) isomers, whereas both azo-Q2a isomers exerted in same inhibition activity against K 4.3, K 2.1, hERG and Ca 1.2 channels (Fig. 5b). Quantification of the inhibition showed that azo-Q2a endows light sensitivity only to Na 1.5 but has negligible effects on K and Ca channels, yielding photoswitching efficacies of 33.1 ± 4.3% for Na 1.5 and far less for the rest channels, of 5.2 ± 1.7% (K 4.3), 3.6 ± 4.2% (K 2.1), 7.9 ± 4.5% (hERG), 7.7 ± 5.4% (Ca 1.2) (Fig. 5h and Supplementary Table 4). To compare the difference in hERG channel inhibition activity between azo-Q2a and quinidine, we repeated these assessments through application of 10 and 30 µM quinidine. APs expected, quinidine showed comparable pharmacological behavior across all tested ion channels without optical control property (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 7b-d). Notably, at 10 µM, cis-azo-Q2a inhibited Na 1.5 and hERG currents by 61.1% and 45.5%, respectively, yielding a Na 1.5/hERG inhibition ratio of 1.34, whereas quinidine produced 8.8% and 71.7% inhibition (ratio 0.12). This corresponds to an approximately 11-fold increase in the Na 1.5/hERG inhibition ratio, indicating an overall enhancement of functional selectivity relative to quinidine (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Table 5).

In addition, we further evaluated the concentration-response relationship of azo-Q2a and quinidine on hERG channels under 365 and 480 nm illumination, which showed that the IC value of azo-Q2a on hERG was 16-fold lower than that of quinidine (Supplementary Fig. 7e-f).

Together, these results demonstrate that azo-Q2a possesses high selectivity for Na 1.5 channels among cardiac ion channels and other Na 1 subtypes, significantly reducing the hERG channel inhibition activity observed with quinidine. These characteristics make azo-Q2a a promising candidate for the development of photoactivated antiarrhythmic therapies.

azo-Q2a reversibly inhibits Na+ currents in rat primary cardiomyocytes.
We next investigated azo-Q2a as an agent for the selective optical control of Na 1.5 channels in rat primary cardiomyocytes. We recorded voltage-gated Na+ and K+ currents from primary ventricular myocytes under 365 and 480 nm illumination (Fig. 5c).

Consistent with our observations in the transient transfection cell experiments, Na+ current in cardiomyocytes was reduced at 365 nm illumination after the addition of azo-Q2a (10 µM), and this was reversed by blue light (480 nm) (Fig. 5d). The selective optical control of Na 1.5 channels was over multiple on/off cycles (Fig. 5d-e); the photoswitching efficacy was 24.3 ± 3.3%, showing no significant difference from the 33.1 ± 4.3% compared to HEK293T cells expressing Na 1.5 channels (Fig. 5h). No significant inhibition on K+ currents were observed under the same experimental conditions (3.0 ± 2.4%), supporting the selectivity of azo-Q2a towards Na 1.5 channels (Fig. 5f-h). Additionally, quinidine (in 10 and 30 µM) was applied as control which showed insignificant optical control of both Na+ (0.8 ± 0.8%) and K+ currents (0.9 ± 1.9%, in 10 µM), (Supplementary Fig. 7b-d). To further exclude potential effects of UV-induced ROS, we performed illumination-only controls (Supplementary Fig. 8a), which showed no changes in sodium currents, consistent with the unchanged inhibition of quinidine under both wavelengths.

Owing to the significant role of Na 1.5 in the action potential of myocardial cells, we directly evaluate the effect of azo-Q2a on cardiac electrophysiology performing whole-cell current-clamp recordings on primary cardiomyocytes to assess the impact of trans and cis-azo-Q2a on cardiac action potential (Supplementary Fig. 8b-e). The results demonstrated that cis-azo-Q2a significantly reduced the dV/dt by 47.2 ± 8.7%, whereas trans-azo-Q2a showed only a modest inhibition of 16.6 ± 1.1%. Furthermore, we observed that cis-azo-Q2a shortened the action potential duration at 50% repolarization (APD ) by 55.2 ± 4.9% whereas trans-azo-Q2a produced only a modest inhibition of 16.6 ± 3.4%. We attribute this shortening primarily to the inhibition of the late sodium current (I ), which is known to modulate repolarization.

Cryo-EM Structure basis for azo-Q2a optical control of Na 1.5 channels.
To assess azo-Q2a binding we obtained a cryo-EM structure for Na 1.5 in complex with azo-Q2a at the resolution of 3.0 Å (Na 1.5S-azo-Q2a) (Supplementary Table 6). Illuminated by 365 nm light, azo-Q2a was photo-induced as the cis isomer before sample preparation. Note also that, seeking to optimize protein expression, we truncated the carboxyl terminal domain and linker between repeats Ⅰ-Ⅱ and Ⅱ-Ⅲ of Na 1.532 (referred to as Na 1.5S, Supplementary Fig. 9).

We first assessed the inhibition activity of quinidine on Na 1.5S using whole-cell patch-clamping recording, yielding an IC value of 44.66 μM in the dark and of 43.80 μM under 365 nm illumination; these values do not differ from the values for Na 1.5WT (Supplementary Fig. 10a, c and Supplementary Table 7). We then examined the optical control of azo-Q2a towards Na 1.5S following the same recording protocols and conditions used for Na 1.5WT and found that azo-Q2a showed the same inhibition activity and optical control property for Na 1.5S and Na 1.5WT (IC = 10.44 µM for cis; 75.41 µM for trans, Supplementary Fig. 10b, d), suggesting that truncation of Na 1.5 does not interfere with the interaction of quinidine or azo-Q2a in the pore domain.

The unambiguous EM densities for cis-azo-Q2a are shown in the blue mesh support that the cis-azo-Q2a molecule bind to the pore domain (Figure 6a, Supplementary Fig. 11a). Similar to quinidine, cis-azo-Q2a is coordinated by both polar and hydrophobic residues from repeats Ⅰ, Ⅲ, and Ⅳ, but distanced from repeat Ⅱ (Fig. 6a-c). In addition, upon comparing our complex structure of Na 1.5S with the reported Na 1.5-quinidine structure31 (PDB ID: 6LQA), we found that the binding sites of azo-Q2a and quinidine differ in the central cavity of the pore domain (Fig. 6b-d): quinidine is likely hydrogen-bonded to Gln371, Thr1417, and Ser1759 and appears to interact with Phe1760 through π-π stacking; cis-azo-Q2a is surrounded by multiple hydrophobic residues from the S6 segments (Fig. 6b-c), among which Val405 appears to interact with the quinolone aromatic ring through a hydrophobic interaction (Fig. 5b-c), while Phe1760 plays an essential role connecting with the azobenzene group through π-π stacking (Fig. 6b-c). The interactions between Phe1760 and the quinoline moiety of quinidine changed to the azobenzene portion of cis-azo-Q2a, while the S6 of Na 1.5S undergoes an α to π helix transition (Fig. 6e, Supplementary Fig. 11b).

We generated Na 1.5 variants bearing on V405A and F1760A mutations, expressed them in HEK293T cells, and assayed azo-Q2a inhibition activity in the dark or under 365 nm illumination. We assessed the inhibitory effect of 100 μM quinidine on the V405A and F1760A mutants. The results demonstrated that the functional impairment was more pronounced in the F1760A mutant compared to the WT, with inhibition rates of 77.6 ± 3.2 % (WT), 51.2 ± 2.3% (V405A), and 32.6 ± 1.8% (F1760A), (Supplementary Fig. 7g). This finding is consistent with previous cryo-EM structural analyses, which revealed that the quinoline ring of quinidine forms critical interactions with the F1760 residue31.

Assessing the calculated concentration-responses supporting our Na 1.5S-azo-Q2a structural insights: Both mutations V405A and F1760A resulted in a significant rightward shift of the IC curve for cis-azo-Q2a (IC > 100 μ M, Fig. 6f–h and Supplementary Table 8), indicating a substantial reduction in its inhibitor potency. Collectively, these findings confirm that Val405 and Phe1760 are critical residues for the binding and inhibition of Na 1.5 by cis-azo-Q2a, thereby establishing them as essential molecular determinants for the light-dependent control mediated by azo-Q2a.

azo-Q2a reversibly attenuates heart rate and terminates ISO-induced tachycardia in vivo in zebrafish larvae.
To assess the capability of azo-Q2a to confer optical heart rate control in vivo, we used zebrafish larvae (2 days post-fertilization) as the animal model (Fig. 7a), for which light scattering is known to be low33. The Na+ current (I ) generated by Na 1.5 channels is essential for maintaining a normal heart rate. Heart rate was monitored by counting the number of sequential contractions in 10-30 s intervals under a dissecting microscope.

The larvae were exposed to different treatments via soaking (Control; 10 μM azo-Q2a and 10 μM quinidine) for 1-1.5 h in the dark34, and then heart rate was recorded 30 min after 365 or 480 nm light exposure using video microscopy (Fig. 7a). We illuminated control zebrafish larvae that we kept under dissimilar experimental conditions for 5 min (at 365 nm or at 365 nm followed by 480 nm light both continuing for 5 min), aiming to estimate optical effects on the heart rate (Fig. 7a).

We first examined the heart rate of larvae treated with no inhibitor as a control: these showed no significant change after different light exposure, suggesting that the light itself does not affect the heart rate (Fig. 7b). The average heart rate of control experiments measured in the dark was used as baseline to normalize each detection value. After perfusion of trans-azo-Q2a (10 μM) lasting for 1-1.5h in the dark, there was no difference in the calculated heart rate (98.8 ± 1.4%) compared to the control (Supplementary Movie 1) treated with DMSO. However, we did observe a significant slowing of the heart rate for these larvae after 365 nm illumination (56.5 ± 4.3%, Supplementary Movie 2), and this slowing was reversed by the subsequent 480 nm illumination (103.2 ± 2.0%, Fig. 7b, Supplementary Table 9 and Supplementary Movie 3).

We also examined larvae perfused with disposed with quinidine in the dark (90.8 ± 1.4%), under 365 nm illumination (93.9 ± 0.9%) and after subsequent 480 nm illumination (91.6 ± 1.3%), (Fig. 7b and Supplementary Table 9). These results are consistent with previous reports for quinidine’s inhibition activity, demonstrating that azo-Q2a confers optical control and has higher inhibition of the heart rate in vivo compared with quinidine35.

To further evaluate the therapeutic potential of azo-Q2a against arrhythmias, we established a tachycardia model in zebrafish larvae (3–4 dpf, untreated control shown in Supplementary Movie 4) by incubating them in darkness with 10 μM isoproterenol (ISO) for 100 min, which significantly increased heart rate36 (Supplementary Movie 5). Using the same treatment and illumination protocol as described above, we found that both 10 μM cis-azo-Q2a (35.3 ± 2.6%, Supplementary Movie 6) and 100 μM quinidine (Supplementary Movie 7) markedly attenuate heart rate in ISO-pretreated larvae, whereas 10 μM trans-azo-Q2a (Supplementary Movie 8) produced only a mild reduction in heart rate (4.4 ± 1.2%, Supplementary Fig. 12). These results demonstrate that light-induced isomerization of azo-Q2a can effectively terminate ISO-induced tachycardia in vivo, thereby supporting its potential relevance for Na 1.5-related arrhythmias.

Overall, these results indicate that the optical control phenomena of electrophysiological experiments obtained in vitro can be reproduced in living animals and moreover, that azo-Q2a can reversibly control heart rate.
paper_content.methods:
Ethics statement
All animal procedures were conducted in strict accordance with the “Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals” and the “Principles for the Utilization and Care of Vertebrate Animals”. All experimental protocols were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Peking University Health Science Center (DLASB D0572). All zebrafish (AB strain) used in this study were raised and handled according to protocol (IMM-XiongwW-3) approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Peking University, which is fully accredited by the Association for Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care International (AAALAC). Every effort was made to minimize animal suffering and to reduce the number of animals used.

Chemical Synthesis and Photochemical Characterizations
azo-QDs were synthesized and characterized by standard chemical methods. The UV-visible absorption spectra of the cis and trans isomers were determined by UV-Vis spectroscopy. 365 nm and 480 nm LED light was used to perform trans ↔ cis isomerization in vitro. Ratio of the trans and cis isomerization and half-life of cis isomerization was determined by NMR spectra. Full design, synthesis, and photochemical characterization of the azo-QDs is detailed in the Supplementary Information.

Cell culture and transfection
The human embryonic kidney cells (HEK293 and HEK-293T) and Chinese hamster ovary cells (CHO) were obtained from ATCC. HEK293 and HEK-293T cells were maintained in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM, Gibco) supplemented with 15 % (volume/volume) Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS, PAN-Biotech) at 37 °C and 5 % CO . In addition, due to poor adherence of HEK293T stable cell lines expressing K 4.3 channels and K 2.1 channels, 0.1 mg/mL Poly-D-lysine (Sigma) was perfused in culture dishes prior to cell culture and the ratio of FBS increased to 20 %. CHO cells were maintained in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium / Nutrient Mixture F-12 (1:1, DMEM/F12, SinoDetech) supplemented with 10 % (volume/volume) FBS.

Cells with 70 ~ 80 % confluence were transiently transfected with plasmid DNA using Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Then the cells were cultured for 20 ~ 48 h and subjected to experiments.

Voltage-clamp recordings
Voltage-clamp recordings were obtained using a HEKA EPC-10 patch-clamping amplifier (HEKA Electronic) and the data were acquired by the PatchMaster program (HEKA Electronic). For whole-cell patch-clamping recording, patch pipettes were pulled from thin-walled borosilicate glass (Sutter Instrument), polished, and gave resistances of 1.5 to 2.5 MΩ in the experimental solutions. In addition, all recordings were accepted only when series resistance was <6 MΩ and compensated by 70%, and seal resistance exceeded＞1 GΩ. To evaluate the inhibition effect of quinidine and azo-QDs, compounds were delivered by gravity perfusion. The illumination during whole-cell patch-clamping recording was given by LumiCite 9100 LED (OPLENIC). For 480 nm wavelength, 100% light intensity was used (45000 lux), and for 365 nm wavelength, 35% light intensity was used (1200 lux).

As for the voltage-clamp recording analyses, all data were reported as mean ± SEM. Data analyses were performed using Origin 2022 (Origin Lab), Excel 2016 (Microsoft), and GraphPad Prism 10 (GraphPad Software). Inhibition curves were generated using a Hill equation (1)
I = Imax / (1+10(logIC50-[C])×H) (1)
where I is the current at different compounds concentrations, I is the maximal current of ion channels without inhibitor application, [C] is the logarithmic concentration, IC is the half-maximal inhibition concentration and H is the Hill coefficient.

Sodium channel
For sodium currents recording, the pipette solution contained 140 mM CsF, 10 mM HEPES, 1 mM EGTA, 10 mM NaCl (pH = 7.3 with CsOH and an osmolarity of ~295 mOsm/L). The bath solution contained 140 mM NaCl, 3 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 10 mM Glucose, 1 mM CaCl , 1 mM MgCl (pH = 7.3 with NaOH and an osmolarity of ~310 mOsm/L). In whole-cell recordings of Na 1.5 currents, the cells were held at −120 mV and the inward peak sodium currents were elicited by a 50 ms step to −20 mV. Recordings from other sodium channel isoforms (Na 1.2–Na 1.6) were performed under the same holding conditions (−120 mV) but using subtype-specific test pulses: 0 mV for Na 1.2 and Na 1.3 (50 ms), −30 mV for Na 1.4 (20 ms), and −10 mV for Na 1.6 (50 ms). In addition, the current-voltage (I–V) relationships were obtained by a 50 ms step from −120 to +40 mV in 5 mV increment. To calculate the voltage dependence of activation, conductance G was fitting with Boltzmann equation (2)
G / Gmax = 1 / (1+e -(Vm-V1/2)/k) (2)
where G is conductance and G is the maximum conductance between −120 and +40 mV. V is the stimulus potential. V indicates the voltage at half-maximal activation, and k is a slope factor describing voltage sensitivity of the channel. k is the slope factor. G are calculated from the I–V relationships according to equation (3)
I = G * (Vm+ENa) (3)
where I is the peak current, G is conductance, V is the stimulus potential, E is the equilibrium potential which is the calculated reversal potential based on our whole-cell recording of Na 1.5 I-V response curve. Significance of fitted V compared to control was analyzed using extra sum-of-squares F test.

Potassium channel
For potassium currents recording, the pipette solution contained 130 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 5 mM EGTA, 1 mM MgCl , 5 mM Mg-ATP (pH = 7.3 with KOH and an osmolarity of ~295 mOsm/L). The bath solution contained 138 mM NaCl, 4 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 10 mM Glucose, 2 mM CaCl , 1 mM MgCl , 0.33 mM NaH PO ·2H O(pH = 7.3 with NaOH and an osmolarity of ~310 mOsm/L). In whole-cell recordings of K 4.3 currents, the cells were held at −80 mV then currents were elicited by a 600 ms step to +60 mV. For hERG currents, the cells were held at −80 mV then currents were elicited by a step to +20 mV following a step to -40 mV, each stimulation last for 2 s40,41. For K 2.1 currents, the cells were held at −80 mV then currents were elicited by a 100 ms step to -120 mV.

Calcium channel
For calcium currents recording, the pipette solution contained 135 mM K-gluconate, 10 mM HEPES, 5 mM EGTA, 2 mM MgCl , 5 mM NaCl, 4 mM Mg-ATP (pH = 7.3 with KOH and an osmolarity of ~295 mOsm/L). The bath solution contained 105 mM NaCl, 30 mM TEA-Cl ,10 mM BaCl ·2H O, 10 mM HEPES, 10 mM Glucose, 5 mM CsCl, 4 mM KCl, 1 mM MgCl (pH = 7.3 with NaOH and an osmolarity of ~310 mOsm/L). In whole-cell recordings of Ca 1.2 currents, the cells were held at −80 mV then currents were elicited by a 200 ms step to -10 mV.

Isolate and culture rat ventricular primary cardiomyocytes
Ventricular primary cardiomyocytes were isolated from 1- to 2-day-old Sprague-Dawley rats42 provided by Peking University Health Science Center Department of Laboratory Animal Science. All animals were handled in strict accordance with the “Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals” and the “Principles for the Utilization and Care of Vertebrate Animals,” and all animal work was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Peking University Health Science Center (DLASBD0572). Each effort was made to minimize animal suffering and the number of animals used. The experiments were blind to viral or drug treatment conditions during behavioral testing. The gender of the fetal rats was not screened during the experiment.

Briefly, primary cardiomyocytes were isolated with 0.05% trypsin (Gibco) and 0.1% collagenase II (Sigma). Cardiomyocytes were separated from the fibroblasts by pre-plating the digested cell suspension for 2 h. Cells were maintained in DMEM (Gibco) supplemented with 10 % (volume/volume) FBS (PAN-Biotech) and antibiotics (100 U/ml penicillin and 100 mg/ml streptomycin) (Gibco) at 37 °C and 5% CO .

The voltage-gated whole-cell patch-clamping recording of sodium and potassium currents in primary cardiomyocytes follow the protocol in HEK293T cells. For cardiac action potential recordings, data were collected using a Multiclamp 700B amplifier (Molecular Devices), filtered at 10 kHz and sampled at 50 kHz. Patch pipettes (3–6 MΩ) were filled with an internal solution containing 130 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 5 mM EGTA, 1 mM MgCl₂, and 5 mM Mg-ATP (pH 7.3 adjusted with KOH; ~295 mOsm/L). The external bath solution contained 138 mM NaCl, 4 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 10 mM glucose, 2 mM CaCl₂, 1 mM MgCl₂, and 0.33 mM NaH₂PO₄·2H₂O (pH 7.3 adjusted with NaOH; ~310 mOsm/L). Series resistance (10–30 MΩ) was compensated by ~60–80%, and recordings were discarded if series resistance varied by more than 20% during the experiment. Action potentials were evoked by 4-ms depolarizing current injections (500 pA) applied at 1 Hz. Data were acquired and analyzed using pClamp 10.4 (Molecular Devices).The maximal upstroke velocity (V ) was determined as the peak of the first derivative of the membrane voltage (dV/dt) during the depolarization phase. APD₅₀ was measured as the time from the overshoot to 50% repolarization.

Heart rate recording in zebrafish
To determine heart rate of zebrafish, 2 dpf embryos were loaded in a recording chamber filled with E3 solution at the desired stage. Heart rate was calculated by counting the number of sequential contractions in 30 s intervals under a dissecting microscope (S8APO; Leica)43. The gender of the embryos was not screened during the experiment. All zebrafish in this study were raised and handled according to a zebrafish protocol (lMM-XionguW-3) approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Peking University, which is fully accredited by the Association for Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care international.

In order to detect the effects of compounds on zebrafish heart rate under different illumination, the control group was without treatment, and the quinidine and azo-Q2a were prepared with E3 buffer at the applicated concentrations. Then, zebrafish larvae were exposed to the compounds by soaking and incubated in a 28.5 ℃ incubator in the dark for 1.5 h under perfusion. Next the heart rate labeled darkness was recorded as described above. After that, giving to each group respectively 365 nm light (4500 Lux) or 365 nm after a subsequent illumination with 480nm light (180000 Lux), the duration of each illumination is 5 minutes. Finally, we recorded the heart rate of groups labeled 365 nm or 365 nm + 480 nm after placing the larvae in the dark for 30min after light exposure.

To further examine the therapeutic potential of azo-Q2a against Na 1.5-related arrhythmia, a tachycardia model was established in 3–4 dpf zebrafish larvae by incubation with 10 μM isoproterenol (ISO) in Hanks’ solution for 100 min in darkness. Following ISO treatment, larvae were exposed to 10 μM cis-azo-Q2a, 10 μ M trans-azo-Q2a or 100 μM quinidine under 365 nm illumination for 5 min or kept in darkness. Heart rate was measured after an additional 30 min of darkness.

Transient co-expression of human Na 1.5S and β1
The methods for transient co-expression, protein purification, cryo-EM analysis were conducted following a standard protocol44. The optimized coding DNAs for human Na 1.5 (Uniprot: Q14524) was cloned into the pEG BacMam vector with twin Strep-tag and FLAG tag in tandem at the amino terminus, while β1 (Uniprot: Q07699) was cloned into the pCAG vector without affinity tag45,46. To optimize the protein behavior, carboxyl terminal domain (1895-2016) and linker between repeat Ⅰ-Ⅱ (461-657) and Ⅱ-Ⅲ (1066-1187) of Na 1.5, named Na 15S, were deleted based on the truncated construct rNa 1.532. HEK293F cells (Invitrogen) were cultured in SMM 293T-I medium (Sino Biological Inc.) under 5 % CO in a Multitron-Pro shaker (Infors, 130 r.p.m.) at 37 ℃. When cell density reached 1.8 ~ 2.2 ×106 cells/ml, 2.0 mg plasmids (1.5 mg Na 1.5S and 0.5 mg β1) and 4 mg of 40-kDa linear polyethyleneimines (PEI, Yeasen) were mixed up in 15 mL fresh medium and pre-incubated for 15- 30 min before adding into 1 liter cell culture. In addition, 10 mM sodium butyrate was added to cell culture. Transfected cells were cultured for 48 h before harvesting.

Protein purification of Na 1.5S and β1
14 liter transfected cells were harvested by centrifugation at 1431 g and resuspended in the lysis buffer containing 25 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5) and 150 mM NaCl. The suspension was supplemented with 1 % (w/v) n-dodecyl-β-D-maltopyranoside (DDM, Anatrace), 0.1 % (w/v) cholesteryl hemisuccinate Tris salt (CHS, Anatrace), and protease inhibitor cocktail containing 2 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (PMSF), 6.5 μg/ml aprotinin, 3.5 μg/ml pepstatin, and 25 μg/ml leupeptin. After incubation at 4 ℃ for 2 h, the cell lysate was centrifuged at 16751 g for 1 h, and the supernatant was applied to anti-Flag M2 affinity gel (Sigma) at 4 °C. After flow through by gravity, the resin was rinsed four times with the Wash buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, 0.02% (w/v) glycol-diosgenin (GDN, Anatrace), and the protease inhibitor cocktail). Protein was eluted with the wash buffer plus 200 μg/mL FLAG peptide (GL.biochem). The eluent was then applied to Strep-Tactin Sepharose (IBA Lifesciences). The purification protocol was similar to the previous steps except for the elution buffer, which was Wash buffer plus 2.5 mM D-Desthiobiotin (IBA Lifesciences). The eluent was then concentrated via 100-kDa cutoff Centricon (Millipore) and further purified with size exclusion chromatography (Superose-6 Increase 10/300 column, GE Healthcare) in Wash buffer. Peak fractions were pooled and concentrated to ∼30 μL. Then, 1 mM azo-QD (effectiveness 82 %) was added to the concentrated sample 30 min before cryo sample preparation.

Cryo-EM data acquisition
4 μl aliquots of concentrated Na 1.5S-azo-Q2a complex were applied to Quantifoil 300 mesh R1.2/1.3 Au grids which were glow-discharged for 35 s at medium RF level of Plasma Cleaner PDC-32G (Harrick). Then grids were blotted from both sides for 4 s at 8 °C and 100 % humidity and plunge-frozen in liquid ethane using a Vitrobot Mark IV (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Prepared grids were subsequently transferred to a Titan Krios electron microscope (Thermo Fisher) operating at 300 kV and equipped with Cs corrector, Gatan K3 Summit detector and GIF Quantum energy filter. A total of 9,406 movie stacks were automatically collected, using AutoEMation47 with a slit width of 20 eV on the energy filter and a preset defocus range from -1.8 µm to -1.5 µm in super-resolution mode at a nominal magnification of 64,000×. Each stack was exposed for 2.56 s with the exposing time of 0.08 s per frame, resulting in total of 32 frames per stack. The total dose rate was 50 e-/Å2 for each stack. The stacks were motion corrected with MotionCor248 and binned 2 fold, resulting in a pixel size of 1.0979 Å/pixel. In addition, dose weighting was performed49. The defocus values were estimated with Gctf50.

Image processing
The data processing procedure was nearly identical to the one we previously reported51. In brief, a total of 6,525,104 particles were automatically picked in cryoSPARC52. 2D classification identified 614,955 good particles that were subsequently applied to Hetero refinement and non-Uniform refinement. Finally, a 3D EM map with an overall resolution of 3.03 Å was generated using 287,376 particles. The resolution was estimated with the gold-standard Fourier shell correlation 0.143 criterion53 with high resolution noise substitution54.

Model building and structure refinement
The initial model of Na 1.5S was based on the coordinate of human Na 1.5-quinidine (PDB:6LQA)31, and the model building and structure refinement processes were the same as we used before51. In brief, the coordinate of Na 15-quinidine was fitted into the EM map by CHIMERA (Detailed workflow were shown in Supplementary Fig. 9b)55. And every residue was manually checked in COOT56 carefully. The chemical properties of amino acids were considered during model building. The cis-azo-Q2a was fitted into the EM map. Structure refinement was performed using phenix.real_space_refine application in PHENIX57 real space with secondary structure and geometry restraints. Over-fitting of the overall model was monitored by refining the model in one of the two independent maps from the gold-standard refinement approach and testing the refined model against the other map58. Statistics of the map reconstruction and model refinement can be found in Supplementary Table 6.

Molecular docking simulation
The Cryo-EM structure of the Na 1.5–cis-azo-Q2a complex was refined in Schrödinger Maestro v13.5, followed by restrained minimization using the Impref module of Impact with the OPLS4 force field, in which hydrogen atoms were optimized while allowing limited heavy-atom relaxation59-61. The trans-azo-Q2a ligand was prepared in LigPrep to generate low-energy, all-atom conformers, with ionization states enumerated at pH 6.5 ± 1.0 and minimized using OPLS461. A receptor grid was defined from the cis-azo-Q2a binding pocket, and trans-azo-Q2a was docked into Na 1.5 in both unconstrained and pose-constrained modes, the latter referencing the cis-azo-Q2a orientation. Docking was performed using Glide in extra-precision (XP) mode, and poses were ranked by GlideScore and evaluated by MM/GBSA to estimate relative binding free energies62.

Data analysis and Statistics
For in vitro experiments, the cells were evenly suspended and then randomly distributed in each well tested. For in vivo experiments, the zebrafish were distributed into various treatment groups randomly. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 10 (GraphPad Software). Before statistical analysis, variation within each group of data and the assumptions of the tests were checked. Comparisons between two independent groups were made using unpaired Student’s two-tailed t test. Comparisons among nonlinear fitted values were made using extra sum-of-squares F test. Comparisons among three or more groups were made using ordinary one-way ANOVA. * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001. Values of IC are presented as mean (95 % CI (Profile likelihood)). Other data are presented as mean ± SEM.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this interesting manuscript, Shiqi Liu and co-workers reported a photoactive inhibitor of the cardiac sodium channel Nav1.5 based on the antiarrhythmic drug quinidine. They presented electrophysiology, cryo-EM structure and living zebrafish in vivo results, demonstrating that the inhibitory activity of azo-Q2a is photoswitchable. The manuscript is clearly written and the experiments are well-performed. This reviewer has several suggestions concerning their figure presentation and the optical control mechanism, which, hopefully, could help the authors to clarify their manuscript. After revision, this reviewer supports its publication in Nature Communications.
Major concerns:
1. Quinidine is an open state blocker of Nav1.5, whether azo-Q2a is also an open state blocker or not?
2. Selectivity. I suggest the author to tune down the selectivity of azo-Q2a. First, it still inhibits hERG as shown in Fig. 4b (45% for hERG and 60% for Nav1.5); second, it is not known the efficiency of azo-Q2a for other sodium channel subtypes.
3. The EM complex structure supports the binding of an optical control blocker in Nav1.5. However, the structure figure is not clearly presented. It’s difficult to interpret the precise interactions between cis-azo-Q2a and the channel, and the detailed differences between cis-azo-Q2a and quinidine. For example, how confident to claim a carbon-hydrogen---π interaction between Val405 and the quinolone ring?
4. EM map. The EM density in Fig. 5b appears to support the binding of cis-azo-Q2a. For clarity, this reviewer suggests that the authors should present the density map of cis-azo-Q2a from three different views, as well as density maps for the S6 helices, because of conformational changes (Fig. 5e).
5. The author used a loop truncated version human Nav1.5S instead of full-length Nav1.5 for improved protein behavior, based on the construct of rNav1.5. Please provide reference.
6. It is not clear how Val405 contributes to the inhibitory activity of azo-Q2a but not optical control, while F1760 determines the optical control as interpreted in Lines 246-255. From the results in Fig. 5f-h, the response of azo-Q2a to V405A and F1760A looks similar under darkness or 365 nm light.
7. The optical control mechanism is unclear. Is it because the cis form of azo-Q2a prefers binding in the identified pocket in Nav1.5 while the trans form could cause steric clashes with the channel, or because of different accessibility for the two forms? The authors should dock the trans form in the pocket and discuss possible molecular mechanism for optical control.
Minor points:
1. In Line 187, Supplementary Fig. 3d should be Supplementary Fig. 3e?
2. In Line 148, what is azo-2P, azo-Q2a, and azo-6M? These names are not consistent in Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 2.
3. In Lines 133, 142, 275 and others, 365nm should be 365 nm.
4. In Line 305, Inhibitors should be inhibitors.
5. In Line 458, what is “NaV1.5Short-azo-Q2a”? Double-check other typos.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors present a photoswitchable quinidine derivative, azo-Q2a, targeting the cardiac sodium channel NaV1.5. While NaV1.5 is essential for cardiac depolarization and quinidine has long-standing utility as an antiarrhythmic agent, its poor specificity and off-target effects—particularly hERG inhibition—limit its clinical use. Through the synthesis of azobenzene–quinidine derivatives, the authors identify azo-Q2a as a lead compound with reversible, light-dependent activity: it is highly potent in its cis form (activated by 365 nm light) and largely inactive in its trans form (480 nm light or dark), demonstrating approximately a 7-fold difference in efficacy. Azo-Q2a exhibits strong selectivity for NaV1.5 over other cardiac ion channels and significantly reduces hERG-related cardiotoxicity relative to quinidine. Cryo-EM structural analysis reveals key binding interactions with NaV1.5, notably involving residues Phe1760 and Val405. In vivo, azo-Q2a enables reversible, light-mediated modulation of heart rate in zebrafish larvae, underscoring its potential as a research tool and therapeutic lead for arrhythmia.
Despite these strengths, the manuscript notably fails to acknowledge significant prior work in this area. In particular, the study omits reference to “Optical Control of Cardiac Electrophysiology by the Photochromic Ligand AzoBupivacaine 2” (Fehrentz et al., Br. J. Pharm., 2025, 82, 1125–1142), which introduced azobupivacaine (AB2) as a reversible photoswitchable NaV1.5 blocker. That earlier work demonstrated optical control of cardiac function in more advanced mammalian models—including mouse left ventricular slices and Langendorff-perfused hearts—and achieved optical termination of ventricular tachycardia. Conceptually, the current study does not extend meaningfully beyond these findings. While the zebrafish data are elegant, they do not surpass the physiological relevance achieved with AB2. The cryo-EM structural data are novel and represent a valuable contribution to mechanistic understanding and future drug design. However, in isolation, they may not justify publication in a high-profile venue, particularly given that azo-Q2a’s action spectrum provides no clear advantage over that of AB2.
In summary, without a thorough acknowledgment of prior work and a demonstrable advance in biological scope or translational relevance, this manuscript is not suitable for publication in its current form in Nature Communications.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In their manuscript, Liu et al. describe the azologization of quinidine and assess the optical control of their most promising analogue, azo-Q2a, both in vitro and in vivo in zebrafish larvae. The approach is scientifically compelling. However, previous studies have largely reported similar strategies and outcomes on other channels or receptors, which reduces the novelty of the current work.
To be considered for publication in Nature Communications, several critical issues must be addressed.
First, in the experimental section, essential information is missing regarding the light intensity used for photoisomerization. Since the efficiency of azobenzene switching is intensity-dependent, the authors must report the irradiance used and the quantum yields for both trans-to-cis and cis-to-trans conversions. These details are crucial for the reproducibility of the study.
Second, the UV-Vis spectra presented in Figure 2 were obtained in MeOH:H₂O, while those in Supplementary Figure 1 were acquired in DMSO. The rationale behind the use of different solvents is not provided. This inconsistency complicates the comparison of isomerization efficiency. The authors should use the same solvent system across experiments and clearly state the solvent and ratio employed in the in vitro and in vivo assays.
Moreover, the kinetics of photoisomerization for azo-Q2a are not reported. Providing the time course for both trans-to-cis and cis-to-trans conversions would significantly strengthen the photochemical characterization.
Regarding chemical synthesis, it would be beneficial to present ^1H-NMR data confirming the structure of azo-Q2a in both trans and cis conformations.
In the main text (line 102), the authors state that Q1 and Q3 exhibit significantly higher inhibition than quinidine at 10 µM, as shown in Figure 1a. However, the data supporting this claim are not clearly presented. This is a potentially important observation, independent of optical control, and should be explicitly detailed.
In Figure 2, the isosbestic point shifts following illumination at 480 nm. The authors should comment on the origin of this shift, which is also observed in Supplementary Figure 1a, as it may reflect photoproduct formation or solvent effects.
Supplementary Figure 2 provides a compelling analysis of sodium current inhibition following trans-to-cis conversion. However, to demonstrate reversibility, it is essential to show that subsequent cis-to-trans conversion restores the initial binding affinity. Furthermore, there is inconsistent nomenclature in the figure panels. For instance, panel a refers to azo-Q1a, while current traces are labeled "azo-2p." It is unclear what "azo-2p" denotes, and consistent compound labeling must be maintained throughout the manuscript and supplemental figures, including line 148.
In Figure 3, the authors should clarify whether the IV and conductance curves were obtained after sequential illumination at 365 nm followed by 480 nm, or only after 480 nm exposure.
The authors appear to use the same electrophysiological conditions for sodium current recordings in HEK cells and isolated cardiomyocytes. However, the sodium current amplitude in cardiomyocytes often precludes proper voltage clamping under high extracellular Na⁺ conditions. The use of reduced Na⁺ concentrations (e.g., 20 mM) is standard to achieve adequate space clamp and reliable measurements. The authors should report the seal, access and series resistance criteria used in their recordings.
In Figure 4b, the authors show that azo-Q2a is less potent than quinidine on the hERG channel, a positive outcome. However, since the two isomers of azo-Q2a differ structurally, it is surprising that both exhibit nearly identical inhibition profiles. Supplementary Figure 3e shows superimposable concentration–response curves and IC₅₀ values for the cis and trans forms.
The legends should be corrected to refer to "concentration" (µM), not "dose" (mg/kg), for in vitro experiments.
The authors should also clarify whether illumination-only controls were performed on isolated cardiomyocytes. These cells are highly sensitive to UV-induced reactive oxygen species (ROS), which could confound interpretation of the data.
As sodium channel inhibition should decrease conduction velocity and shorten ventricular action potential duration, direct measurement of these parameters—preferably in neonatal cardiomyocytes or even in ex vivo hearts—would considerably strengthen the physiological relevance of the study.
The structural data presented in Figure 5 are promising, showing cryo-EM of Nav1.5 in complex with cis-azo-Q2a. However, the figure does not clearly depict the molecular interactions between azo-Q2a and the channel. It is also unclear which moieties of azo-Q2a engage in binding. Did the authors test whether quinidine-mediated inhibition is altered in V405A or F1760A mutants? Given that the two isomers of azo-Q2a exhibit different affinities, the authors should indicate whether cryo-EM structures were also obtained for the trans isomer. Such data would be highly informative regarding the structural basis of photoswitchable control. The authors suggest that V405 plays a minor role in optical control based on the small effect observed in the mutant, but this conclusion seems overstated given the limited evidence.
The zebrafish methods lack clarity. It is not clear whether the compounds were bath-applied or microinjected into the larvae. While the authors convincingly show that azo-Q2a can modulate heart rate in vivo, they do not include results for 100 µM quinidine, a concentration known to inhibit multiple ion channels. The lack of effect observed with quinidine is mentioned but not supported by citations. Moreover, the hypothesis that increasing selectivity toward sodium channels would enhance bradycardia is questionable and requires a more nuanced explanation.
Have the authors tested whether repeated cycles of 365/480 nm illumination can reproducibly modulate heart rate in larvae? Demonstrating reversibility and repeatability is essential for potential translational applications.
In terms of pharmacokinetics, the in vivo stability of azo-Q2a must be addressed. Azobenzenes can undergo reductive degradation in biological environments; therefore, azo-Q2a sensitivity to GSH, a physiologically relevant reducing agent, should be evaluated.
The authors claim that azo-Q2a could be useful for treating Nav1.5-related arrhythmias. However, none of the current data support this application. Experiments demonstrating that light-induced isomerization can terminate arrhythmias—either in cell-based models or ex vivo heart preparations—would significantly increase the study's impact.
Finally, the authors state (line 318) that red-shifted azobenzene analogs failed to retain optical control of Nav1.5. This is a key point and should be backed by experimental data. If these experiments were performed, the corresponding results must be provided, at least in the Supplementary Information.
Minor comments:
•There are multiple typographical and grammatical errors throughout the text and figure legends that need to be corrected.
•It is not clear whether the authors used calculated or experimentally determined reversal potentials to derive ENa.
•The rationale for choosing +20 mV to activate hERG channels is unclear. Higher test voltages typically provide more robust activation.
•Line 241 incorrectly states that the IC₅₀ of the cis isomer decreased. In fact, the IC₅₀ increased, indicating reduced affinity.
•Lines 303–304: capitalization errors need correction.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors present a photoswitchable quinidine derivative, azo-Q2a, targeting the cardiac sodium
channel NaV1.5. While NaV1.5 is essential for cardiac depolarization and quinidine has long-
standing utility as an antiarrhythmic agent, its poor specificity and off-target effects—particularly
hERG inhibition—limit its clinical use. Through the synthesis of azobenzene–quinidine derivatives,
the authors identify azo-Q2a as a lead compound with reversible, light-dependent activity: it is
highly potent in its cis form (activated by 365 nm light) and largely inactive in its trans form (480 nm
light or dark), demonstrating approximately a 7-fold difference in efficacy. Azo-Q2a exhibits strong
selectivity for NaV1.5 over other cardiac ion channels and significantly reduces hERG-related
cardiotoxicity relative to quinidine. Cryo-EM structural analysis reveals key binding interactions
with NaV1.5, notably involving residues Phe1760 and Val405. In vivo, azo-Q2a enables reversible,
light-mediated modulation of heart rate in zebrafish larvae, underscoring its potential as a research
tool and therapeutic lead for arrhythmia.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's positive feedback on the achievements presented
in this manuscript. We would like to further highlight the key novel aspects of our work, which
include:
1. The first synthesis of a series of new photoswitchable Na 1.5 channel blockers derived
V
from quinidine;
2. A unique photoswitchable inhibition behavior between the cis-active and trans-inactive
forms of azo-Q2a againstNa 1.5 but no other channels, by exhibiting a 7-fold difference
V
in activity;
3. The first Cryo-EM structure of Na 1.5 in complex with the cis-active isomer azo-Q2a,
V
which reveals key binding interactions and paves the way for designing next-generation
photoswitchable Na 1.5 channel blockers.
V
Despite these strengths, the manuscript notably fails to acknowledge significant prior work in this
area. In particular, the study omits reference to “Optical Control of Cardiac Electrophysiology by
the Photochromic Ligand AzoBupivacaine 2” (Fehrentz et al., Br. J. Pharm., 2025, 82, 1125–1142),
which introduced azobupivacaine (AB2) as a reversible photoswitchable Na 1.5 blocker. That
V
earlier work demonstrated optical control of cardiac function in more advanced mammalian
models—including mouse left ventricular slices and Langendorff-perfused hearts—and achieved
optical termination of ventricular tachycardia. Conceptually, the current study does not extend
meaningfully beyond these findings. While the zebrafish data are elegant, they do not surpass the
physiological relevance achieved with AB2. The cryo-EM structural data are novel and represent a
valuable contribution to mechanistic understanding and future drug design. However, in isolation,
they may not justify publication in a high-profile venue, particularly given that azo-Q2a’s action
spectrum provides no clear advantage over that of AB2.
Response: We thank the reviewer for bringing this reference to our attention and appreciate their
perspective on its relevance. However, we respectfully suggest that the interpretation of the study
“Optical Control of Cardiac Electrophysiology by the Photochromic Ligand AzoBupivacaine 2” (Br
J Pharmacol. 2025;182(5):1125-1142) may mislead certain aspects, as outlined below:
1. Lack of structural novelty: The compound azobupivacaine (AB2) featured in the
referenced study is not a novel entity; it was previously introduced by the Trauner group
(ACS Chem Neurosci. 2018;9(12):2886-2891).
2. Lack of channel selectivity: As demonstrated in both Leippe et al. (ACS Chem Neurosci.
2018;9(12):2886-2891) and Fehrentz et al., AB2 exhibits concurrent photoswitchable
activity across various channels (e.g., K 2.1, TREK1, Na 1.5), indicating limited
V V
selectivity under light irradiation. Specifically, Fehrentz et al. reported only a 1.4-fold
photoswitching effect on Na 1.5, which prompts questions about the compound's practical
V
effectiveness as a selective photoswitchable modulator for this channel.
In summary, while the work by Fehrentz et al. represents a valuable attempt to explore
photoswitchable Na 1.5 blockers using AB2, the compound’s limited photoswitching performance
V
across different channels (K 2.1, TREK1, and Na 1.5) and between its cis and trans isomers
V V
underscores the challenges in developing highly effective photoswitchable Na 1.5 blockers. This
V
highlights the need for novel compound designs and a deeper mechanistic understanding of
photoswitching behavior. We are pleased that our current work addresses these challenges and
contributes to the rational design of photoswitchable Na 1.5 channel blockers.
V
In summary, without a thorough acknowledgment of prior work and a demonstrable advance in
biological scope or translational relevance, this manuscript is not suitable for publication in its
current form in Nature Communications.

of their most promising analogue, azo-Q2a, both in vitro and in vivo in zebrafish larvae. The
approach is scientifically compelling. However, previous studies have largely reported similar
strategies and outcomes on other channels or receptors, which reduces the novelty of the current

addressed.

V
the predominant cardiac sodium channel, which facilitated a structure-based design aimed at

resolved the cryo-EM complex of azo-Q2a with Na 1.5, revealing key interacting residues and

providing mechanistic insights that may inform the development of next-generation
photoswitchable Na 1.5 inhibitors.

observed for the cis and trans isomers of azo-Q2a can be attributed to fundamental structural
differences between the Na 1.5 and hERG channels. As our cryo-EM data reveal (Fig. 5), the light-
V

V

analogous structural motif thus cannot distinguish between them. Consequently, we assume that

response curves. This outcome highlights a key advantage of azo-Q2a: it delivers highly targeted
photocontrol by activating only on channels with the requisite molecular determinants, thereby
minimizing off-target effects.

applied or microinjected into the larvae.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting this lack of clarity in the zebrafish methods. The
compounds were delivered via bath application (soaking), rather than micro-injection. We have
clarified this point in the revised manuscript to ensure methodological transparency and reliability:
“Then, zebrafish larvae were exposed to the compounds by soaking and incubated in a 28.5 ℃
incubator in the dark for 1.5 h under perfusion.” (Page 19, Line 515-517)
Question: While the authors convincingly show that azo-Q2a can modulate heart rate in vivo, they
do not include results for 100 µM quinidine, a concentration known to inhibit multiple ion channels.
The lack of effect observed with quinidine is mentioned but not supported by citations. Moreover,
the hypothesis that increasing selectivity toward sodium channels would enhance bradycardia is
questionable and requires a more nuanced explanation.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer for raising this point. In our optical control assays evaluating
azo-Q2a’s effect on zebrafish heart rate, the cis-azo-Q2a isomer exhibited significant retard activity
(57 ± 4.3% inhibition, Fig. 6b). Based on this pronounced effect, we selected 10 μM quinidine as a
negative control to benchmark the baseline inhibitory activity of the parent compound under
equivalent experimental conditions. This concentration demonstrated weak heart rate suppression
(94 ± 0.9% under 365 nm, 92 ± 1.3% under 480 nm), consistent with previously reported data
showing low efficacy (88 ± 5%) at 10 μM in zebrafish models. (J Appl Toxicol. 2012;32(10):834-
842)
In addition, we apologize for any lack of clarity in our original manuscript. Our hypothesis posits
that the enhanced bradycardic effect of cis-azo-Q2a lies primarily in its increased efficacy against
the Na 1.5 current, rather than an improvement in channel selectivity. The superior selectivity
V
profile of azo-Q2a over quinidine, however, confers a significant advantage by minimizing off-
target interactions, thereby reducing potential side effects.
Question: Have the authors tested whether repeated cycles of 365/480 nm illumination can
reproducibly modulate heart rate in larvae? Demonstrating reversibility and repeatability is
essential for potential translational applications.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful suggestion. In our zebrafish assay system, we
have successfully demonstrated the optical reversibility of azo-Q2a effect. Specifically, the heart
rate of larvae inhibited by cis-azo-Q2a under 365 nm illumination was rapidly and completely
reversed upon subsequent 480 nm exposure (Fig. 6). While repeated cycles of 365/480 nm
illumination could not be performed because the larvae require a 30 min of recovery after each
illumination to stabilize heart rate, given their sensitivity to light stimulation. This inherent
limitation of the experimental system prevents us from directly demonstrating repeatability across
multiple cycles of lighting of heart rate modulation in vivo.
Question: In terms of pharmacokinetics, the in vivo stability of azo-Q2a must be addressed.
Azobenzenes can undergo reductive degradation in biological environments; therefore, azo-Q2a
sensitivity to GSH, a physiologically relevant reducing agent, should be evaluated.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this constructive comment. GSH can influence azo compounds
in two ways: (i) by mediating the reductive cleavage of the nitrogen–nitrogen double bond, and (ii)
by catalyzing cis-to-trans isomerization. We have experimentally examined both effects, The results
indicated that the half-life of trans-azo-Q2a in 10 mM GSH reduction was 143 minutes, whereas
the half-life for the isomerization of cis-azo-Q2a in 1 mM GSH was 59 minutes (Supplementary
Figure 5). Notably, the isomerization catalyzed by 10 mM GSH was too rapid to be reliably
quantified. As an alternative, we measured the catalytic rate in a 1 mM GSH buffer solution. We
have revised our wording in the revised manuscript as following:
“Finally, we examined the chemical stability of azo-Q2a. Under in vitro conditions, azo-Q2a
remained remarkably stable, exhibiting a half-life (t ) of 107 h in the absence of reducing agents
1/2
(Fig. 2e). In contrast, exposure to 1 mM glutathione (GSH) triggered rapid cis-to-trans
isomerization with a half-life of 59 min, driven by the reversible reduction of the -N=N- bond. At a
higher GSH concentration (10 mM), azo-Q2a underwent predominant reductive degradation with
a half-life of 143 min, indicating a shift in the reaction pathway under strongly reducing conditions
(Supplementary Fig. 5).” (Page 6, Line 155-162)

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors have done a superb job in addressing all the concerns from me and other referees. In my opinion, the revised manuscript has been substantially strengthened. I strongly support publication of this interesting work.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:

"Optical Control of Cardiac Electrophysiology by the Photochromic Ligand AzoBupivacaine 2" Fehrentz, T.; Amin, E.; Görldt, N.; Strasdeit, T.; Moussavi-Torshizi, S. E.; Leippe, P.;Trauner, D.; Meyer, C.; Frey, N.; Sasse, P.; Klöcker, N. British J. Pharm., 2025, 82, 1125-1142.
It is unethical to completely ignore this work. I find it hard to believe that the authors ignored this aspect of my review and chose not to cite and discuss prior art.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors have replied to almost all of my previous comments and have added substantial and valuable data to the revised manuscript. I appreciate the quality of their additional experiments and the effort made to strengthen the study. Nevertheless, I have a few remaining remarks that could further improve the clarity and completeness of the manuscript.
1. Isosbestic point (Figure 2):
I agree with the authors that the slight shift of the isosbestic point could result from minor side- or photoproduct formation or from changes in solvent polarity and ionic strength. It would be helpful to include one brief sentence in the text acknowledging this possible explanation.
2. Recording solutions for HEK cells and cardiomyocytes:
I remain somewhat surprised that cardiomyocytes can be well clamped under the conditions used, given the large ionic gradient applied. A short justification or discussion of how good voltage control was ensured under these conditions would improve the transparency of the electrophysiological methodology.
3. Depolarization rate (Supplementary Figure 8c):
It would be appreciated if the authors could present dV/dtmax values instead of (or in addition to) the “Inhibition of depolarization rate” currently shown. This parameter would provide a more direct and quantitative measure of the effect on excitability.
4. Repeatability in zebrafish experiments:
The authors could mention as a limitation the lack of repeatability in zebrafish assays, which may arise from the high sensitivity of larvae to light stimulation. Including this point would clarify the practical challenges associated with the in vivo experiments.
5. Supplementary Figure 12 – Heart rate quantification:
I acknowledge the authors for adding these new and informative data. It would be of interest to include quantitative comparison of heart rate in the “ISO-trans-azoQ2a” (darkness) condition versus “ISO-cis-azoQ2a.” Such data would strengthen the physiological interpretation of the observed effects and confirm whether the two illumination states indeed differ functionally.

We sincerely thank the reviewers for allowing us to submit a revised version of our manuscript. All modifications have been clearly highlighted. We believe this second round of revisions has significantly strengthened the manuscript and hope it now meets the high standards of Nature communications for publication. Our point-by-point responses follow.
Point-by-point response to reviewers’ comments
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have done a superb job in addressing all the concerns from me and other referees. In my opinion, the revised manuscript has been substantially strengthened. I strongly support publication of this interesting work.
Response:
We sincerely thank reviewer for their strong support and positive assessment of our revisions. We are pleased that the reviewer finds the manuscript substantially strengthened and suitable for publication. A final proofread has been conducted to ensure clarity and consistency throughout the manuscript.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This paper cannot be published without citing thee previous, pioneering work by Fehrtentz, Trauner, and Klöcker and putting it into context:
"Optical Control of Cardiac Electrophysiology by the Photochromic Ligand AzoBupivacaine 2" Fehrentz, T.; Amin, E.; Görldt, N.; Strasdeit, T.; Moussavi-Torshizi, S. E.; Leippe, P.;Trauner, D.; Meyer, C.; Frey, N.; Sasse, P.; Klöcker, N. British J. Pharm., 2025, 82, 1125-1142.
It is unethical to completely ignore this work. I find it hard to believe that the authors ignored this aspect of my review and chose not to cite and discuss prior art.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for their feedback and for highlighting this important prior work. We fully agree on the ethical importance of properly citing and contextualizing relevant literature. We have incorporated the pioneering study by Fehrentz et al. (British Journal of Pharmacology, 2025, 182, 1125-1142) as reference 23 in the current manuscript. This citation appears in the introduction (lines 90-94), where we discuss it in detail as follows:
“Preliminary attempts at photoswitchable modulation of cardiac sodium channels have been reported, while it shows low photoswitching (1.4-fold) at Na 1.5 and poor selectivity over other channels23. This underscores the need for development of novel photoswitchable modulators with higher Na 1.5 selectivity, stronger photoswitching efficacy and clearer mechanistic definition.”
Reference:
23.Fehrentz, T. et al. Optical control of cardiac electrophysiology by the photochromic ligand azobupivacaine 2. Br J Pharmacol 182, 1125-1142 (2025).
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have replied to almost all of my previous comments and have added substantial and valuable data to the revised manuscript. I appreciate the quality of their additional experiments and the effort made to strengthen the study. Nevertheless, I have a few remaining remarks that could further improve the clarity and completeness of the manuscript.
Response:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's positive feedback on the additional data and our overall revisions. We are encouraged that the reviewer finds the newly added experiments substantial and valuable. In accordance with the remaining suggestions, we have carefully implemented further revisions to enhance the clarity and rigor of the manuscript. Our point-by-point responses are detailed below.
Question: Isosbestic point (Figure 2):
I agree with the authors that the slight shift of the isosbestic point could result from minor side- or photoproduct formation or from changes in solvent polarity and ionic strength. It would be helpful to include one brief sentence in the text acknowledging this possible explanation.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for their agreement with our explanation regarding the slight shift in the isosbestic point. As suggested, we have incorporated a brief sentence acknowledging this possibility into the manuscript as following: (lines 151-154 in the revised text)
“While we noted that the isosbestic point shifts slightly upon illumination at 480 nm which is small relative to the main spectral features, this might result from minor side- or photoproduct formation or from changes in solvent polarity and ionic strength.”
Question: Recording solutions for HEK cells and cardiomyocytes:
I remain somewhat surprised that cardiomyocytes can be well clamped under the conditions used, given the large ionic gradient applied. A short justification or discussion of how good voltage control was ensured under these conditions would improve the transparency of the electrophysiological methodology.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that ensuring robust voltage-clamp quality is essential for reliable electrophysiological data interpretation, particularly given the large ionic gradients involved in sodium channel recordings. In our experiments with rat primary ventricular cardiomyocytes, cells were held at a hyperpolarized potential of –120 mV, where Na 1.5 channels (with an activation threshold around –70 mV) remain predominantly in the closed resting state. This minimizes voltage-dependent sodium currents during seal formation, promotes a stable baseline, and facilitates effective clamp control prior to channel activation during test pulses. To enhance methodological transparency, we have added a brief justification to the Methods section in the revised manuscript (lines 469-474).
“In whole-cell recordings of Na 1.5 currents, the cells were held at −120 mV and the inward peak sodium currents were elicited by a 50 ms step to −20 mV. Recordings from other sodium channel isoforms (Na 1.2–Na 1.6) were performed under the same holding conditions (−120 mV) but using subtype-specific test pulses: 0 mV for Na 1.2 and Na 1.3 (50 ms), −30 mV for Na 1.4 (20 ms), and −10 mV for Na 1.6 (50 ms). ”
Question: Depolarization rate (Supplementary Figure 8c):
It would be appreciated if the authors could present dV/dtmax values instead of (or in addition to) the “Inhibition of depolarization rate” currently shown. This parameter would provide a more direct and quantitative measure of the effect on excitability.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. In response, we have incorporated the maximal upstroke velocity (dV/dtmax) values into Supplementary Figure 8c. The original percentage inhibition data for dV/dtmax have been retained in panel 8d to offer complementary insights. This revision provides a more direct and quantitative assessment of the compound's impact on cardiomyocyte excitability, as recommended.

Each line represents paired measurements from the same cell. d, Percentage inhibition rate of the dV/dtmax by 10 μM cis-azo-Q2a and trans-azo-Q2a (n = 3–5). Data are presented as mean ± SEM.
Question: Repeatability in zebrafish experiments:
The authors could mention as a limitation the lack of repeatability in zebrafish assays, which may arise from the high sensitivity of larvae to light stimulation. Including this point would clarify the practical challenges associated with the in vivo experiments.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. We have added a statement in the Discussion section explicitly acknowledge this methodological constraint. This requirement poses an inherent limitation on the repeatability of optical manipulations for controlling heart rhythm in this model.”

Response:
We thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. We have performed additional zebrafish experiments and quantitative analyses comparing the heart rates under the ISO-trans-azo-Q2a and ISO-cis-azo-Q2a conditions, as now detailed in the revised Supplementary Figure 12. The new analysis reveals that under isoproterenol (ISO)-induced tachycardia, heart rate inhibition by trans-azo-Q2a was 4.4 ± 1.2%, whereas cis-azo-Q2a produced a significantly greater inhibition of 35.3 ± 2.6%. This result intuitively provides direct physiological evidence that the functional efficacy of azo-Q2a is markedly dependent on its photoisomeric state, with the cis-configuration being essential for potent heart rate inhibition.
Supplementary Figure 12 | Light-induced termination of ISO-induced tachycardia in zebrafish larvae.
a, Experimental protocol for tachycardia modeling and treatment in zebrafish larvae (3–4 dpf). Larvae were incubated in 10 μM ISO in Hanks’ solution for 100 min in darkness to induce tachycardia, then treated with 10 μM trans-azo-Q2a, 10 μM cis-azo-Q2a or 100 μM quinidine, and subsequently exposed to 365 nm illumination or kept in darkness (5 min), followed by 30 min darkness before final recordings. b, Heart rate measurements showing significant ISO-induced tachycardia (green, n = 27), its reduction by cis-azo-Q2a (violet, n = 23) and quinidine (grey, n = 21), and the mild decrease observed with trans-azo-Q2a (blue, n = 18). Data are shown as mean ± SEM.
